title_original: Johanna Hedva Keeps Doom in Her Mouth
excerpt_original: In her book of essays and fiction, the artist’s sentences shine as blades ground sharp against the void, writing with a mystic orientation to life that tacitly grapples with the question: What is art, or writing, good for now?

blocks.caption: Cover of My Knife Collection and Other Subjects of Desire (2026) by Johanna Hedva (all images courtesy Sming Sming Books)

blocks.text: "Age seven, I stepped barefoot on a slug in the front yard … I will never forget the way my spine shivered and I knew I was in an unknowable presence and I felt my foot never afterwards be clean. Was this God?" This is a perfect origin story for Johanna Hedva's writing. The Korean-American artist ’s sentences shine as blades ground sharp against the void, writing with a mystic orientation to life — mystic but not mystical. The union with otherness here is no easy one. As Hedva says, "I can only use language like fated and chthonic and words that try to reach into the ontological fact that we're ancient and we're fucked." Because "hope, uplift, and transcendence are not to my taste."

For those of us who attend to it closely, and who refuse to leave it alone, life is long . One's relation to it is never not broken, worn, frayed, sullied. It is what can "not be fixed but only endured." Hedva asks, "For people like me, what kinds of spirituality deal with this, not as a salve for the friction but the music made from it?" There's a space for kinds of art, ritual, magic, writing which gesture toward a knowledge that is strictly impossible but at least knows it’s impossible. Hedva again: "I want to hear the voice throw itself against the silence, keep making noise against the asphyxiating black sauce of cosmic noiselessness."

Hedva's work has accumulated a following. As she puts it, "I began to notice that a murder of wayward girls, misfits, freaks, and orphans was circling behind me." The most interesting people, of course. The words that drew them are compiled in My Knife Collection and Other Subjects of Desire (2026), offering her writing in a range of forms: fiction, essays on artists ranging from Tracey Emin to Mire Lee, and short pieces that read a bit like fairytales, but not the Disney kind. There are no happy endings or easy exits for Hedva; "I did not know how I was going to bear this life."
